analogy.p: Think of the glucose as the **cash that a building company earns each day**. Some cash is spent straight away on wages and fuel (**respiration**), some is paid into a secure savings account that does not change the company's day-to-day running (**starch and oils**), some is spent on steel girders and walls (**cellulose**), and some is spent on machinery that needs a special ingredient bought from a supplier (**proteins**, which need nitrate ions from the soil). The savings can be withdrawn when business is slow, like starch broken down at night or in winter. The analogy breaks down because money is just swapped between accounts, whereas in a plant glucose is chemically converted into different molecules, and respiration releases energy rather than just spending a token.

bullets: Learn the **five uses**: respiration, starch, fats/oils, cellulose, amino acids/proteins.
Know that **nitrate ions from the soil** are needed to make proteins.
Know **why** starch is stored (insoluble) and what cellulose does (strengthens cell walls).
Be able to describe glucose use from a **data table, bar chart or pie chart** and do simple percentage calculations.
Recall the **iodine test for starch** (orange-brown to blue-black).
Link to **photosynthesis**, **respiration**, **active transport** and **plant mineral deficiencies**.
Typical marks: 1 mark to name a use, 2 marks to explain why, 4 marks for a short extended answer.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.4.1.3 says that the **glucose produced in photosynthesis may be used in several ways**: for **respiration**, converted into **insoluble starch for storage**, used to produce **fat or oil for storage**, used to produce **cellulose**, which strengthens the cell wall, and used to produce **amino acids for protein synthesis**. To make proteins the plant also needs **nitrate ions absorbed from the soil**. This is a short list that gives easy marks if each use is linked to a reason, and it connects photosynthesis to respiration, transport and plant nutrition.

bullets: Glucose is made in the **chloroplasts** of leaf cells during photosynthesis.
Glucose contains only **carbon, hydrogen and oxygen**, so to make **proteins** (which need nitrogen) extra elements are needed from the soil.
Plant **biomass** (the mass of living material) is built from glucose and minerals, so more photosynthesis leads to more growth.
The glucose may be **used immediately** or **converted** into other molecules for **storage or building**.
Dissolved sugars are moved around the plant by the **phloem** to wherever they are used or stored.
Photosynthesis only happens in the light, but **respiration and storage continue all the time**.
The uses are not exclusive: at any time a plant is using glucose in **several ways at once**.
core.h: Where the glucose comes from and the big picture
core.p: Plants make **glucose** in photosynthesis (carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen), using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll. Glucose is a simple sugar, but a plant needs many other substances to live and grow, so it uses glucose as a **starting material and an energy source**. A plant is **not** able to take in food: it must make everything it needs from glucose and the minerals it takes from the soil. This is why glucose is described as the plant's main product, and why all of the biomass of a plant ultimately comes from photosynthesis.

bullets: Aerobic respiration: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water** (and energy is released).
Symbol equation: **C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O**.
It happens in the **mitochondria** of **every living cell** of the plant, **day and night**.
Energy released is used for **active transport** (e.g. mineral ions into root hair cells), **protein synthesis**, **cell division and growth**.
The energy is **released**, not 'made'; it comes from the chemical energy stored in glucose.
In the light, some of the CO₂ from respiration is reused by photosynthesis; in the dark, the plant gives out CO₂ from respiration.
Mark scheme link: respiration is the process that **transfers energy from glucose**, which is what plants need to carry out their life processes.
core.p: Plants use some of the glucose they make for **respiration**, the process that **releases energy** for the plant's life processes. Respiration occurs in the **mitochondria** of **all living cells**, in the light and in the dark. The equation for aerobic respiration is **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water** (energy is released). The energy is used for **active transport** of mineral ions into the roots, for making large molecules such as proteins and cellulose, and for growth and cell division. It is an important point that plants **both photosynthesise and respire**, and they respire all the time.

bullets: Starch is a **polymer** of glucose: **many glucose units joined in a long chain**.
Starch is **insoluble**, so it **does not dissolve in the cell's water** or change the concentration of the cell contents.
Because it does not affect **osmosis**, cells can store large amounts of starch without water moving in and making the cell burst or swell.
It is a **compact** store: lots of glucose in a small space.
Stored in **roots, tubers (potato), seeds (cereal grain), stems and leaves**.
Starch is **broken down into glucose** by enzymes when the plant needs energy or materials.
**Iodine test:** add iodine solution to the sample: **orange-brown → blue-black** if starch is present.
Animals store glucose as **glycogen**, not starch (comparison point).
core.p: Plants convert glucose into **starch** for storage. Starch is made of **many glucose molecules joined together in long chains**, and it is **insoluble** in water, which makes it ideal for storing. Plants store starch in their **roots, stems, leaves and seeds**, for example in potato tubers, and use it later when photosynthesis cannot supply enough glucose (at night, in winter, or when a seed germinates). When glucose is needed again, **enzymes break the starch down** into glucose.

bullets: Cellulose is made from **glucose** and forms the **cell wall** of plant cells.
Its function is to **strengthen the cell wall** and **support** the cell and plant.
Cell walls are made of **long fibres** arranged in layers, giving **high tensile strength**.
The cell wall is **fully permeable**, but stops the cell **bursting** when it takes in water.
Growth needs a lot of cellulose because **new cells** have to build new walls.
Cellulose is **not** the same as starch: both come from glucose but have **different arrangement and function** (support vs storage).
Humans cannot digest cellulose; it forms **dietary fibre**.
The **bacterial cell wall** is **not** made of cellulose.
core.p: Plants use glucose to make **cellulose**, a substance that **strengthens the cell wall**. Cellulose is also made of **long chains of glucose units**, but the chains are arranged into **strong fibres** that criss-cross the wall. The cell wall surrounds the cell membrane and **supports the cell and the whole plant**. The wall also stops cells from bursting when water enters by osmosis, so the cell becomes firm (turgid). Cellulose is therefore one of the main uses of glucose in a **growing plant** because every new cell needs a new cell wall.

bullets: **Glucose + nitrate ions → amino acids → proteins.**
**Nitrate ions** provide the **nitrogen** that glucose does not contain.
Nitrate ions enter root hair cells by **active transport** (needs energy from **respiration**).
Proteins are used for **enzymes**, **growth**, **repair** and as parts of **cell structures**.
**Nitrate deficiency** causes **stunted growth** because the plant cannot make enough protein.
**Fertilisers** (containing nitrate, phosphate and potassium) are added to soil to replace nitrates removed by crops.
The amino acids are joined in a **specific order** to make a particular protein.
Link: plants that live in nitrate-poor soils may have special adaptations (e.g. root nodules in legumes, covered elsewhere).
core.h: Use 4: amino acids, proteins and nitrate ions
core.p: Plants use glucose to make **amino acids**, which are then joined together to make **proteins**. Because glucose contains no nitrogen, plants must also take in **nitrate ions from the soil**, which supply the nitrogen needed for amino acids. The nitrate ions enter the **root hair cells** by **active transport**, which needs energy from respiration because the ions are absorbed against a concentration gradient. Proteins are needed for **growth and repair**, to make **enzymes**, and as structural components of cells such as membranes. Without nitrate the plant cannot make enough protein.

bullets: Fats and oils are **lipids**: **fats** are solid at room temperature, **oils** are liquid.
They are made from **glucose** (the plant converts glucose into **glycerol and fatty acids**).
They are an **energy-rich store**, often in **seeds** (e.g. sunflower seeds, rapeseed, nuts).
Stored energy supports the **germination** of the seed until the new plant can photosynthesise.
Lipids are **insoluble in water**, so they do not affect water balance of cells.
Per gram, fats and oils store **more energy than carbohydrate** such as starch.
Used by humans as **cooking oil**, margarine and in food manufacture.
core.h: Use 5: fats and oils for storage
core.p: Plants also convert some glucose into **fats or oils** for storage. Fats and oils are **energy-rich**: they store more energy per gram than starch, so they are a compact way of storing energy, particularly in **seeds**. Sunflower, rapeseed, olive and many nuts contain oils, which supply energy to the embryo during germination until it can photosynthesise. The oils are also useful to humans for **cooking and food**. Like starch, they are insoluble in water and so do not affect osmosis in the cell.

bullets: **Phloem** carries **dissolved sugars** (e.g. **sucrose**) from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
This movement is called **translocation**.
Phloem moves materials in **both directions**; xylem carries water and minerals **upwards**.
Sugars may be **used** (respiration, growth) or **stored** (starch, oils) where they arrive.
Storage organs include **roots, tubers, seeds and fruits**.
Phloem cells are **living** and use **energy from respiration** (companion cells).
Sugars are often moved as **sucrose**, which is soluble and can be transported in solution.
Link: see **plant tissues** (xylem and phloem) in the organisation topic.
core.h: Transport: moving the glucose around the plant
core.p: Glucose is made in the leaves but is needed all over the plant: in the roots, the growing shoot tips, the flowers and the fruits. The plant therefore **transports dissolved sugars (often as sucrose)** through the **phloem** from where they are made (the leaves) to where they are needed or stored. This is called **translocation**. The phloem is living tissue and can carry substances in **both directions**, unlike the xylem, which carries water and minerals upwards only. Phloem transport is the link between photosynthesis in the leaf and the uses of glucose elsewhere in the plant.

bullets: **Respiration:** releases energy now, **in mitochondria**; uses glucose and oxygen.
**Starch:** stores glucose, **insoluble**, used later for respiration.
**Fats/oils:** stores a larger amount of energy per gram, especially in **seeds**.
**Cellulose:** forms the **cell wall**, giving strength and support.
**Amino acids/proteins:** need **nitrate ions**; make **enzymes and structures**, support growth.
Energy uses: respiration (now), starch and oils (later).
Building uses: cellulose and proteins (growth).
A plant does **all of these at the same time**, but the amounts change with the age and needs of the plant.
core.h: Comparing the five uses of glucose
core.p: It helps to compare the five uses side by side because exam questions often ask you to match a use with its function or explain why a plant needs it. **Respiration** releases energy, **starch** and **fats/oils** store energy for later, **cellulose** builds structure, and **amino acids** build proteins. The first two groups are about energy, and the others are about building materials. Some of the products also supply energy later, since starch is broken down to glucose and oils can be respired.

bullets: Dissolved glucose would **increase the solute concentration** and draw in water by **osmosis**.
**Insoluble** starch and oils do **not dissolve**, so they do not change the water balance.
Many glucose molecules are packed into a **single large molecule** (starch), which is a compact store.
Insoluble stores **cannot leak out** of cells, unlike glucose, which can diffuse across membranes.
Stored energy can be **released** when enzymes break starch back into glucose.
Link to **osmosis** in the transport topic: water moves from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
A common exam answer is **'starch is insoluble so it does not affect the water potential / osmosis in cells'**.
core.h: Why insoluble storage molecules make sense
core.p: A plant cell is surrounded by water, and the movement of water in and out of cells depends on the **concentration of dissolved substances**. If the glucose were stored as dissolved glucose, the cell would become very concentrated and water would move in by **osmosis**, which could damage the cell. **Starch and oils are insoluble**, so they have almost **no effect on osmosis**, and a cell can hold a large reserve without disturbing its water balance. They are also **compact**, so a store of energy takes up little space.

bullets: **Producers** make their own food by photosynthesis; their **biomass** supports the food chain.
Photosynthesis **transfers light energy** to chemical energy stored in glucose, starch and other molecules.
Respiration **releases** that stored energy for the plant's life processes.
Only a part of the glucose goes into **new biomass** (growth); the rest is used in respiration.
The carbon in biomass came from **atmospheric CO₂** by photosynthesis (the **carbon cycle**).
Increasing the rate of photosynthesis (limiting factors) increases the glucose available for **growth and yield**.
Plants are **producers**; animals eat the starch, sugars, proteins and oils that the plants have made.
core.p: Photosynthesis and respiration are closely linked. Photosynthesis **stores energy** in glucose and other organic molecules, and respiration **releases** that energy for the plant. The substances that the plant builds from glucose make up its **biomass**, which is the food for **herbivores** at the start of every food chain. Nearly all of the energy in food chains comes from the light that was absorbed in photosynthesis, so plants are called **producers**. A good extended answer may link the uses of glucose to growth, food and the carbon cycle.

bullets: **Mass from a percentage:** mass = percentage ÷ 100 × total (40% of 200 g = 0.40 × 200 = **80 g**).
**Percentage of total:** part ÷ total × 100 (60 g of 200 g = 60 ÷ 200 × 100 = **30%**).
**Remainder:** total − sum of known parts (200 − 80 − 30 − 20 − 10 = **60 g**).
Check that the percentages in a pie chart **sum to 100%**.
Describe data with **figures and units** and use comparatives (more than, less than).
When asked for the **largest use**, compare the actual values.
Pie chart angle for a percentage: **percentage × 3.6°** (e.g. 40% = 144°).
**Mean** of repeats is used if measurements (e.g. starch tests) are repeated.
core.h: Data and maths skills for this topic
core.p: You may be given a table, pie chart or bar chart showing how a plant uses its glucose, or a graph of mass over time. Typical calculations are **percentages of a total**, **mass from a percentage** and comparing values. When you describe data, quote figures with units and compare them. A good way to check a pie chart is to make sure the percentages add up to **100%**.

bullets: **Respiration (4.4.2):** glucose is used in aerobic respiration to release energy.
**Active transport:** root hair cells absorb **nitrate ions** against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
**Osmosis:** insoluble starch does not change the concentration of the cell, so osmosis is unaffected.
**Plant tissues:** the **phloem** moves dissolved sugars from the leaf to storage organs.
**Mineral deficiency:** **nitrate** deficiency → **stunted growth**; **magnesium** deficiency → **chlorosis** (yellow leaves).
**Fertilisers** supply nitrate, phosphate and potassium for plant growth.
**Digestive enzymes:** carbohydrases (amylase) break starch down in animals; plants have enzymes that break their own starch down.
**Biodiversity/food security:** efficient use of glucose affects crop yield.
core.h: Links to other topics and plant mineral deficiencies
core.p: The uses of glucose connect to many other topics: **respiration** (energy release), **active transport** (nitrate uptake), **osmosis** (why starch is insoluble), **plant tissues** (phloem transport) and **enzymes** (breakdown of starch). Plants also need other **mineral ions**. **Nitrate deficiency** causes stunted growth, and **magnesium deficiency** causes yellowing leaves (**chlorosis**) because magnesium is needed to make **chlorophyll**. Understanding the uses of glucose also helps you to understand why farmers add fertiliser and why crops need nitrate.

exam: **State uses of glucose (1 mark each):** respiration; starch (storage); fats/oils (storage); cellulose (cell walls); amino acids (proteins). Name the use, do not just write 'energy'.
**Explain why starch is stored (2 marks):** insoluble (1), so does not affect osmosis / does not dissolve in cell contents (1); can be broken down to release glucose.
**Cellulose (1-2 marks):** used to make cell walls (1) which strengthen the cell/support the plant (1).
**Proteins (3 marks):** glucose is used to make amino acids; nitrate ions from the soil are needed; amino acids are joined to make proteins.
**Nitrate uptake (3 marks):** by root hair cells by active transport, against a concentration gradient, using energy from respiration.
**Iodine test (2 marks):** add iodine solution (1); orange-brown to blue-black means starch is present (1).
**Calculations (2-3 marks):** show the percentage/mass working (e.g. 40% of 200 = 0.4 × 200 = 80 g) and include units.
**Pie charts/tables:** quote figures with units; make sure percentages add up to 100%.
**Link questions:** be ready to link to respiration (mitochondria), osmosis, active transport and the phloem.
**Command words:** *State/Name* = short; *Explain* = give a reason (because...); *Describe* = what happens; *Give one use* = just one, specific use.
**Common 4-mark format:** use, reason, link to cell/plant need, then an example (e.g. potato tuber).

mistakes.r: Glucose is also used to make starch, fats/oils, cellulose and amino acids.
mistakes.w: Plants use glucose only for respiration.

mistakes.r: Plants respire all the time, day and night, in the mitochondria of all living cells.
mistakes.w: Plants do not respire because they photosynthesise.

mistakes.r: Respiration releases energy from glucose; energy is not made.
Starch is stored because it is insoluble, so it does not affect osmosis and can be stored compactly.
mistakes.w: Starch is stored because it is soluble and easy to move.

mistakes.r: Cellulose strengthens the cell wall (support); starch, fats and oils are the storage molecules.
Nitrate ions supply nitrogen to make amino acids and proteins; energy comes from respiration of glucose.
mistakes.w: Plants take in nitrates for energy.

mistakes.r: Nitrate ions are absorbed by active transport against the concentration gradient, using energy from respiration.
mistakes.w: Nitrate ions enter the root by osmosis or diffusion.

mistakes.r: Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present.
mistakes.w: Iodine turns black to orange when starch is present.

mistakes.r: Plants make their own proteins from amino acids, which they make from glucose and nitrate ions.
mistakes.w: Plants get proteins from the soil.

summary: AQA 4.4.1.3: you must know that glucose from photosynthesis is used for respiration, converted into insoluble starch for storage, made into fats or oils for storage, used to make cellulose for cell walls, and used to make amino acids for protein synthesis with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil. It matters because it links photosynthesis to respiration, plant growth, storage and mineral nutrition, and it is tested with short recall questions and percentage calculations.

terms.d: A simple sugar made in photosynthesis; the starting material for many substances in the plant.
The process, in the mitochondria of all living cells, that releases energy from glucose.
An insoluble carbohydrate made of many glucose units, used for storage.
A carbohydrate made from glucose that strengthens the cell wall.
The rigid layer outside the cell membrane in plant cells that strengthens and supports the cell.
Small molecules containing nitrogen that are joined together to make proteins.
The making of proteins by joining amino acids in a specific order.
Mineral ions absorbed from the soil that supply nitrogen for making amino acids and proteins.
Energy-rich lipids made from glucose and used for storage, e.g. in seeds.
Plant tissue that transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
The movement of dissolved sugars in the phloem.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration, e.g. nitrate ions into root hair cells.
The mass of living material in an organism.
The reagent used to test for starch; turns from orange-brown to blue-black.
An organism, such as a plant, that makes its own food by photosynthesis.
The start of growth of a seed into a new plant, using stored food.
Poor, reduced growth, a symptom of nitrate deficiency.

worked.q: A plant makes 200 g of glucose in one day. 40% is used in respiration, 15% for cellulose, 10% for amino acids and 5% for fats and oils. The rest is stored as starch. Calculate (a) the mass used in respiration, (b) the mass stored as starch, (c) the percentage stored as starch. (4 marks)
steps: Mass for cellulose = 0.15 × 200 = 30 g; amino acids = 0.10 × 200 = 20 g; fats and oils = 0.05 × 200 = 10 g.

worked.ans: Model answer: Nitrate ions provide the nitrogen needed to make amino acids, which are made from glucose and nitrate and then joined together to make proteins for growth and enzymes. Nitrate ions enter the plant through root hair cells by active transport, which moves them against a concentration gradient using energy released by respiration.
worked.q: Explain why plants need nitrate ions and how nitrate ions enter the plant. (4 marks)
steps: Purpose: nitrate ions supply nitrogen that is needed to make amino acids (glucose has no nitrogen).
Amino acids are joined to make proteins (needed for growth, enzymes).
Entry: absorbed by root hair cells.
Process: active transport, against the concentration gradient, using energy released by respiration.

worked.ans: Model answer: Starch is insoluble so it does not affect water movement by osmosis and is a compact store that can be broken down into glucose when needed. To test for starch, add iodine solution to a slice of the tuber; it turns from orange-brown to blue-black if starch is present.
worked.q: A potato tuber stores glucose as starch rather than as glucose. Explain why this is an advantage to the plant. Describe how to test a tuber slice for starch. (4 marks)
steps: Starch is insoluble, so it does not dissolve in the cell contents.
Therefore it does not affect osmosis: water does not move into the cell and make it swell or burst.
It is a compact store of many glucose units that can be broken down to glucose later.
Test: add iodine solution to the slice; orange-brown turns blue-black if starch is present.
